summary:
Fire Harmonizer solves a problem every fire-monitoring team runs into: NASA's two active-fire sensors, MODIS and VIIRS, don't agree. Different pixel size (1km vs 375m) and saturation temperature mean VIIRS detects 3-6x more fire pixels than MODIS in published comparisons (5.13x over 10 years in South America, 4.8x in Punjab, India), with MODIS underestimating fire radiative power by over 42% in parts of Africa. That gap hides real signal: is a spike a true surge, or one sensor seeing what the other missed?

Our tool stops forcing users to pick a sensor. A live Region Picker lets anyone draw a box anywhere on Earth and pull real-time, combined MODIS and VIIRS counts from NASA FIRMS. A Dashboard runs a 75-day case study over Kazakhstan, our local event's region, scoring each day with an unsupervised Isolation Forest model on each sensor's count, gap, and ratio, with no faked accuracy number, since no ground truth exists here.

A review of 11 peer-reviewed papers confirmed no universal correction factor exists between these sensors; recalibration is region and platform specific. So we built a transparent, honest anomaly layer on real NASA data, a live, global tool turning two disagreeing feeds into one trustworthy signal.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Fire Harmonizer turns two disagreeing NASA fire sensors, MODIS and VIIRS, into one honest, usable signal. It has two live tools and one offline analysis:

- Region Picker: draw a box anywhere on Earth on a live map, pick a date and range, and get real-time combined MODIS + VIIRS hotspot counts for that exact area, pulled straight from NASA FIRMS.

- Fire Activity Dashboard: a 75-day case study (Sept 1 to Nov 14, 2026) over Kazakhstan, our local event's region, showing MODIS vs VIIRS counts side by side, their gap and ratio, real NASA GIBS satellite snapshots per day, and a downloadable CSV of the underlying hotspot data for that window.

- An offline machine learning layer that scores each day's sensor disagreement and flags the days worth a second look.

HOW IT WORKS

The browser never talks to NASA directly. An Express.js backend holds the FIRMS API key server-side and proxies every request, so the key never reaches client code. The Region Picker calls this proxy live, on demand, for any bounding box the user draws with Leaflet and Leaflet.draw. The Dashboard is precomputed: 75 days of FIRMS CSV data and GIBS imagery are pulled once, scored offline, and preloaded into the page, so judges see instant results with no live-request fragility during a demo.

The scoring layer uses an unsupervised Isolation Forest (scikit-learn), trained fresh on each run, not a pretrained model. It has no labeled ground truth to learn from, because none exists for this comparison, so it is never framed as an accuracy score. It is framed for what it actually measures: how far a day's MODIS/VIIRS disagreement (count, gap, ratio) sits from the seasonal baseline. A rule-based tier (good, warning, serious, critical) makes that score legible to a non-technical reader.

WHY WE BUILT IT THIS WAY

We read 11 peer-reviewed remote-sensing papers before writing a line of fusion logic. The literature is clear that VIIRS and MODIS disagree by a lot and inconsistently: VIIRS detected 5.13x more fire pixels than MODIS over 10 years in South America, 4.8x more in Punjab, India, and MODIS underestimates fire radiative power by over 42% in parts of Africa. It is equally clear that no single correction factor generalizes: fitted coefficients from one satellite pair do not transfer to another without recalibration, and the VIIRS/MODIS relationship itself shifts with spatial scale. Rather than inventing a universal fix the science does not support, which the literature treats as the harder and less honest path, we built a transparent anomaly layer that reports disagreement truthfully. We think that choice, defensible science over an impressive-looking but unsupported formula, is the real creative contribution here.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Fire managers, researchers, and local monitoring groups currently cross-reference two raw NASA feeds by hand to tell a real fire surge from a sensor artifact. Fire Harmonizer does that work automatically, for any region on Earth, not just the one we demo. The Kazakhstan case study shows how it applies to local wildfire and agricultural burning seasons specifically, but the Region Picker is global by design.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Data integrity: no fabricated accuracy numbers, no synthetic ground truth, every figure traceable to a real NASA endpoint or a cited paper.

- Accessibility: chart and calendar colors use a colorblind-safe palette, not a default rainbow scheme.

- Demo reliability: motion libraries are self-hosted, not loaded from a CDN, so a flaky connection during judging cannot break the page; the historical dashboard needs no live network call at all.

- Privacy and security: the FIRMS API key lives only on the server; it is never shipped to the browser.

- Accessibility of motion: every animation, from the map's zoom transitions to the page's entrance effects, respects a visitor's reduced-motion preference.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, AND SOFTWARE

Node.js and Express.js for the backend proxy; vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the frontend; Leaflet and Leaflet.draw for the interactive map; GSAP for motion design; Python and scikit-learn (Isolation Forest) for the anomaly model; NASA FIRMS (MODIS NRT and VIIRS NOAA-20 NRT) and NASA GIBS as the live data sources; deployed on Vercel.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A tool that a real fire-management or research team could use today, not a demo that only works for one country or one date range, and a reminder that the more credible answer in science is usually "the data disagree, and here is by how much," not a single clean number that papers over the disagreement.
